subject: confirmation-bias
title: Confirmation Bias: Test to Fail
summary: Why smart people get stuck on wrong answers, and how scientists and founders fight it.

keys.prompt: Why can't testing 11, 13, 15 show your "+2" rule is wrong, and what test can?
keys.answer: It fits your rule, so "fits" teaches nothing new. A triple that breaks your rule, like 11, 12, 19, can surprise you.

keys.prompt: What is confirmation bias, and when is it strongest?
keys.answer: Favoring information that supports what you already believe; strongest for outcomes you want, emotional topics and long-held beliefs.

keys.prompt: What was Klayman and Ha's point about positive tests?
keys.answer: Positive tests are often informative; Wason's task was a special case where the true rule was broader than people's guesses.

cards.title: Smart and still stuck
cards.text: In a famous experiment, smart adults spent ages "proving" a rule that was wrong, and every test they ran told them they were right. How is that possible?

cards.question: In a famous experiment, smart adults kept "proving" a wrong rule. What do you think went wrong?

options.text: They only tested examples that fit their guess

cards.reveal: They only ran tests that fit their own guess, like 11, 13, 15 for "+2 each time." A "fits" can't surprise you. A test like 11, 12, 19 can.

cards.title: The 2-4-6 task
cards.text: In Peter Wason's 1960 experiment, people were told that 2, 4, 6 fits a rule. They proposed number triples and heard "fits" or "doesn't fit." Many announced rules far more specific than the real one, such as "the middle number is the average of the other two."
cards.example: The real rule: any ascending sequence. If you think the rule is "+2 each time," testing 11, 13, 15 can't show you're wrong. Testing 11, 12, 19 can.

cards.title: What it is
cards.text: Confirmation bias is the tendency to search for, interpret, favor, and recall information in a way that supports what you already believe. It's strongest for outcomes you want, emotionally charged topics, and beliefs you've held a long time.

cards.title: Why founders should care
cards.text: Research links confirmation bias to flawed decisions in business, finance, and science, and to overconfidence. If you only ask friends whether they'd buy your product, you are running the 11, 13, 15 test.

why.q: Why is asking your friends whether they'd buy your product a weak test?
why.a: Friends tend to agree with you, so a "yes" can't surprise you. It's the 11, 13, 15 test.

examples_by_interest.golf: Say you think a new putter fixed your putting. If you only remember the putts you made, you're running the 11, 13, 15 test. Count every putt, made or missed.
examples_by_interest.soccer: Say you think your team plays better in blue jerseys. Remembering only the wins in blue is the 11, 13, 15 test. Track every game, win or lose.

cards.title: A twist
cards.text: Testing examples that fit your idea isn't always bad. Researchers Klayman and Ha argued that positive tests are often informative in real life. The trap in Wason's task was that the true rule was much broader than people's guesses, so "fits" answers taught them nothing new.

cards.prompt: Socrates showed people they didn't know what they thought they knew. How is designing a test that could fail a Socratic move?
cards.model: Both go looking for the question or test that could break your belief, instead of the ones that confirm it.

cards.question: Pick a belief you have about your golf swing, a team, or a business idea. Design one test that could prove you wrong. What result would actually change your mind?
nudges: Decide in advance what would count as "wrong."
Who could you ask that would not just agree with you?

questions.q: You think the rule is "+2 each time." Which test is most informative?

options.why: It breaks your rule. If it still fits, your rule is too narrow.
It fits your rule, so a "fits" answer can't surprise you.

questions.q: When is confirmation bias strongest, per research summaries?

options.text: For desired outcomes, emotional issues, and deeply held beliefs
options.why: Right. Caring a lot makes it harder to see clearly.
It shows up everywhere, especially on things we care about.
Adults and experts show it too.

questions.q: What was Klayman and Ha's point?

options.text: Positive tests are often informative; Wason's task was a special case where the true rule was broad.
options.why: Yes. The real skill is choosing tests that can surprise you.
They refined the explanation; they didn't deny the pattern.
Their critique was about the strategy, not the numbers.

cards.prompt: Explain this to someone at dinner in 3 sentences.
